comparison: Both strongly support the core finding that ΔrecA strains develop accelerated antibiotic resistance (C3, C27-C31). OpenEval emphasizes convergent experimental evidence across multiple methods, while peer reviewers explicitly affirmed this as 'a valuable observation' with 'convincing' data. High agreement on this central claim.

OpenEval R1 includes C25-C26 (independent ΔrecA strains showing similar phenotype), which peer R2 addresses separately. Both support these claims; peer reviewers noted the systematic testing without challenge. Partial overlap with full agreement.

Both address statistical analysis of mutation mechanisms (C32-C40). OpenEval emphasizes rigorous statistical methods distinguishing mutation rate from selection. Peer reviewers initially raised concerns about selection vs. mutagenesis but accepted the fluctuation analysis after revision, stating 'the authors have addressed my major concerns.' Agreement achieved after revision.

OpenEval R2 includes statistical claims (C86-C90) that peer R10 incorporates into the broader mechanistic model. Both support the interpretation that selection dominates over elevated mutation rate. Peer reviewers accepted this after revisions addressed initial concerns about methodology.

Very high overlap (C41-C46, C49-C51) on WGS findings identifying specific resistance mutations in ampC, PBP3, and AcrB. Both strongly support these findings. Peer reviewers described the mutations in detail and confirmed initial WGS methodology concerns were addressed in revision. Strong agreement.

OpenEval R3 includes C105 (cross-resistance to other antibiotics), which peer R15 addresses. Both support this finding; peer reviewers noted 'mutations conferring resistance to ampicillin are also increasing resistance to other antibiotics.' Agreement on cross-resistance phenomenon.

Perfect overlap on SOS-independence claims (C52-C55). Both strongly support the finding that other SOS pathway deletions do not replicate the ΔrecA phenotype. Peer reviewers highlighted this as 'a major strength' and found it 'surprising' that SOS response is not involved. Strong agreement.

OpenEval R4 includes C91 (SOS-independent mechanism), which peer R11 incorporates into the broader mechanistic synthesis. Both support this interpretation as part of the overall model distinguishing this pathway from canonical SOS-mediated mutagenesis.

Perfect overlap on microscopy findings (C57-C60) showing reduced DNA Pol I recruitment. Both support these findings. Peer reviewers noted the observation is 'valuable for the field' despite mechanistic gaps. OpenEval also emphasizes RNA-seq support (C71, C78, C92-C93) not explicitly discussed in peer R6.

OpenEval R5 includes C71 (repair pathway suppression) which peer R7 addresses through transcriptomic analysis. Both support downregulation of repair genes. Peer reviewers found these observations 'useful for more detailed mechanistic follow-ups.' Agreement on transcriptomic evidence.

OpenEval R5 includes C78 (antioxidant gene suppression) which peer R8 addresses as part of the ROS mechanism. Both support this finding as contributing to elevated ROS and mutagenesis. Agreement on transcriptomic basis for ROS accumulation.

OpenEval R5 includes C92-C93 (SOS-independent repair suppression) which peer R11 incorporates into the mechanistic synthesis. Both support this as part of the overall model explaining how RecA loss affects repair independently of SOS.

Very high overlap (C61-C72) on RNA-seq analysis showing downregulation of antioxidant and repair genes. Both strongly support these findings with appropriate statistical thresholds. Peer reviewers found the transcriptomic data 'useful' and accepted it as part of the mechanistic framework. Strong agreement.

OpenEval R6 includes C94 (repair pathway suppression) which peer R11 incorporates into the mechanistic synthesis. Both support the transcriptomic evidence for compromised DNA repair as part of the dual-mechanism model.

High overlap (C73-C79) on ROS-mediated mutagenesis and GSH rescue experiments. Both strongly support these findings. Peer reviewers highlighted the GSH experiment as particularly convincing evidence that ROS drives resistance evolution. OpenEval emphasizes the elegant decoupling of mutagenesis from killing; peer reviewers accepted the ROS mechanism. Strong agreement.

OpenEval R7 includes C7, C82-C83 (ROS contribution to mutation supply) which peer R10 incorporates into the dual-mechanism model. Both support ROS as a key driver of mutagenesis in the ΔrecA background, integrated with selection dynamics.

OpenEval R7 includes C95-C97 (ROS and repair defects as mechanistic basis) which peer R11 incorporates into the overall mechanistic synthesis. Both support the integrated model of compromised repair and oxidative stress driving resistance evolution.

Perfect overlap on H-NS upregulation (C80-C81). Both rate this as UNCERTAIN due to speculative mechanism. OpenEval notes the causal connection requires experimental validation; peer reviewers implicitly accepted the transcriptomic data but did not explicitly evaluate the mechanistic proposal. Agreement on uncertainty.

High overlap (C98-C102) on H-NS mechanism. Both rate as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval emphasizes need for H-NS deletion/overexpression validation; peer reviewers note this 'remains to be experimentally validated' per authors' own acknowledgment. Strong agreement on speculative nature requiring further validation.

High overlap (C4, C8, C10-C11, C85, C89) on the dual-mechanism model integrating mutation supply and selection. Both strongly support this synthesis. Peer reviewers accepted the model after revisions, noting it introduces 'new concepts to antimicrobial resistance evolution mechanisms.' Agreement on the integrated mechanistic framework.

Perfect overlap on high-level conclusions (C12, C103). Both support these as justified by experimental evidence. Peer reviewers called it 'a valuable observation' and 'a nice mechanistic contribution.' OpenEval notes other claims in R10 are more speculative, which peer R12 does not address.

High overlap (C104, C106, C109-C110) on therapeutic implications. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to speculative nature requiring clinical validation; peer reviewers SUPPORTED these as reasonable implications without challenge, noting translational relevance to antimicrobial resistance. Divergence: OpenEval more cautious about clinical applicability, peer reviewers accept as logical extensions.

OpenEval R10 includes C107 (generalization to other antimicrobial approaches) which peer R15 addresses. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN requiring validation; peer reviewers SUPPORTED as logical extension without challenge. Divergence in confidence about generalizability.

OpenEval R11 addresses background literature and context claims (C1-C2, C13-C24, C84). No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers focused on experimental findings rather than literature review accuracy. OpenEval confirms these accurately represent established knowledge.

OpenEval R12 addresses established molecular biology context (C47-C48, C56). No corresponding peer review evaluation found, as reviewers did not explicitly evaluate background knowledge claims. OpenEval confirms these are appropriately cited and accurate.

Peer R15 addresses cross-resistance and generalization (C105, C107-C108). OpenEval addresses C105 in R3 (SUPPORTED) and C107 in R10 (UNCERTAIN). Peer reviewers supported the cross-resistance findings and accepted generalization without challenge, while OpenEval was more cautious about broader applicability.
